title: The universal subject
summary: Every real sentence has a main carriage and an engine; when the main carriage is not spoken it is a zero pronoun, not a missing subject.

blocks.text: Some teachers say Japanese has no subject, because so many sentences seem to start with nothing. This course disagrees: every real sentence says something (the engine) about something (the main carriage). Japanese is a **null-subject** language, like Spanish: the subject is not always visible, but it is there.

The invisible main carriage is found from context, and when context says nothing it defaults to **I**. Spanish does the same: "Soy americana" drops "yo" because "soy" already says it. English "am" also implies "I", but English forbids dropping it.
It is not that "tiredness hangs over the universe". A language must be able to say something about something.
Some subjects are vague, as English "it" is. The copula だ links two things, so a hidden first thing must be there: here it is "it", the weather or the day.

blocks.en: It looks like rain. ("it" is the hidden main carriage)

blocks.text: 雨になりそうだ。 The copula still links two things.
A noun with a long modifier is not a sentence. You see these in game recaps, chapter titles and narration.

blocks.en: me, who had arrived at the station

blocks.text: 泣いていた子供。 No engine, so no sentence.
There is no main carriage and engine here: just a noun with a modifier.

items: Every real sentence has a main carriage and an engine.
When the main carriage is not spoken it is a zero pronoun: context decides, **I** by default.
A noun with a modifier is not a subjectless sentence; it is not a sentence at all.

questions.instruction: What is a null-subject language?
options: One whose subjects are not always visible
questions.note: The subject is still there.

questions.instruction: What is the hidden main carriage here?
questions.note: The copula needs two things to link, so a hidden "it" is there.

questions.instruction: What does the zero pronoun default to in context-free sentences?
questions.note: When nothing else is clear, it is the speaker.

questions.instruction: True or false?
questions.prompt: Japanese has no subject because the subject is often missing.
questions.note: It is often invisible, not absent.

questions.instruction: Who did it?
questions.note: With no other clue, the zero pronoun is I.
questions.en: "What about the homework?" "(I) already did it."

questions.instruction: Tap the engine (the main carriage is a zero pronoun)
questions.note: 会った is the engine; (I) is the invisible main carriage.
questions.en: (I) met a friend at the station yesterday.

questions.instruction: Who is sleepy in this sentence said on its own?
questions.note: The invisible main carriage defaults to I.

questions.instruction: Who is the zero pronoun here?
questions.prompt: A: 先生は？　B: もう帰りました。
questions.note: Context says A asked about the teacher.
questions.en: A: What about the teacher? B: (He) already went home.

questions.instruction: Which of these is a noun with a modifier, not a sentence?
questions.note: It ends in a noun and says nothing (B) about an main carriage.

questions.instruction: Why isn't this a sentence?
options: It is a noun with a modifier: it says nothing about an main carriage
questions.note: A noun with a modifier has no A and B.
questions.en: the person I met at the station

questions.instruction: Tap the noun that the modifier describes
questions.note: 人 is just a noun with a modifier: not a sentence.
questions.en: the person I met in the park yesterday

questions.instruction: Tap the main carriage
questions.note: 妹が is the main carriage; 来た is the engine.
questions.en: My younger sister came to the station yesterday.

questions.instruction: Which train shows 眠い。 correctly?
questions.note: The main carriage is a zero pronoun, invisible but present.

questions.instruction: Who fell asleep?
questions.prompt: お母さんが赤ちゃんを見て、「寝た」と言った。
questions.note: Context fills the zero pronoun: the baby.
questions.en: Mother looked at the baby and said, "(He) fell asleep."

questions.instruction: Build the sentence
questions.note: Topic, adverb, then the engine; the main carriage (I) is zero.

questions.instruction: Build the sentence
questions.prompt: I read the book I bought yesterday.
questions.note: 買った describes 本; 読んだ is the only engine.
questions.en: I read the book I bought yesterday.

questions.instruction: Which sentence has a zero pronoun?
questions.note: Only 早く寝た。 leaves its main carriage unspoken.

questions.instruction: True or false?
questions.prompt: 窓を開けた人 is a complete sentence.
questions.note: It is a noun (人) with a modifier.
questions.en: the person who opened the window

questions.instruction: Which sentence has a vague "it" as its main carriage?
questions.note: The hidden carriage is "it", the weather.

questions.instruction: Why does this feel complete in Japanese?
options: The zero pronoun (usually I) is the main carriage
questions.note: The main carriage is invisible but still there.

questions.instruction: Build the sentence
questions.note: The hidden main carriage is "it"; 降りそうだ is the engine.

questions.instruction: Who is tired?
questions.note: With no other clue, the zero pronoun is I.
